claim: Reinforcement Learning (RL) models can explain behavior from simple conditioning to complex problem solving.
source: Reinforcement Learning (RL) models have revolutionized the cognitive and brain sciences, promising to explain behavior from simple conditioning to complex problem solving, to shed light on developmental and individual differences, and to anchor cognitive processes in specific brain mechanisms.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by the broader literature context provided in the manuscript.

claim: Many contradictions in the RL literature arise from two commonly-held assumptions about computational model parameters that are actually often invalid: that parameters generalize between contexts and that they capture interpretable neurocognitive processes.
source: We hypothesized that many contradictions arise from two commonly-held assumptions about computational model parameters that are actually often invalid: That parameters generalize between contexts (e.g. tasks, models) and that they capture interpretable (i.e. unique, distinctive) neurocognitive processes.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the study, tested through empirical data collection and analysis.

claim: 291 participants aged 8–30 years completed three learning tasks in one experimental session.
source: To test this, we asked 291 participants aged 8–30 years to complete three learning tasks in one experimental session, and fitted RL models to each.
evidence: This describes the study design and sample.

claim: Some parameters (exploration / decision noise) showed significant generalization: they followed similar developmental trajectories, and were reciprocally predictive between tasks.
source: We found that some parameters (exploration / decision noise) showed significant generalization: they followed similar developmental trajectories, and were reciprocally predictive between tasks.
evidence: This is a main finding from the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Generalization of exploration/decision noise parameters was significantly below the methodological ceiling.
source: Still, generalization was significantly below the methodological ceiling.
evidence: This finding is based on comparison with simulated agents showing perfect generalization.

claim: Other parameters (learning rates, forgetting) did not show evidence of generalization, and sometimes even opposite developmental trajectories.
source: Furthermore, other parameters (learning rates, forgetting) did not show evidence of generalization, and sometimes even opposite developmental trajectories.
evidence: This is a main finding from the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Interpretability was low for all parameters.
source: Interpretability was low for all parameters.
evidence: This is a main finding from the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The systematic study of context factors (e.g. reward stochasticity; task volatility) will be necessary to enhance the generalizability and interpretability of computational cognitive models.
source: We conclude that the systematic study of context factors (e.g. reward stochasticity; task volatility) will be necessary to enhance the generalizability and interpretability of computational cognitive models.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: RL models can explain simple cognitive processes such as stimulus-outcome and stimulus-response learning.
source: RL models can explain not only simple cognitive processes such as stimulus-outcome and stimulus-response learning (Schultz et al., 1997; O'Doherty et al., 2004; Gläscher et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RL models can explain highly complex processes, including goal-directed, temporally extended behavior.
source: but also highly complex processes, including goal-directed, temporally extended behavior (Ribas-Fernandes et al., 2011; Daw et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RL models can explain meta-learning.
source: meta-learning (Wang et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: RL models can explain abstract problem solving requiring hierarchical thinking.
source: and abstract problem solving requiring hierarchical thinking (Eckstein and Collins, 2020; Botvinick, 2012; Collins and Koechlin, 2012; Werchan et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RL models have been applied across the lifespan.
source: RL models have been applied across the lifespan (van den Bos et al., 2018; Bolenz et al., 2017; Nussenbaum and Hartley, 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RL models have been applied in both healthy participants and those experiencing psychiatric illness.
source: and in both healthy participants and those experiencing psychiatric illness (Huys et al., 2016; Adams et al., 2016; Hauser et al., 2019; Ahn and Busemeyer, 2016; Deserno et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A specialized network of brain regions, including the basal ganglia and prefrontal cortex, implement computations that mirror specific components of RL algorithms, including action values and reward prediction errors.
source: A specialized network of brain regions, including the basal ganglia and prefrontal cortex, implement computations that mirror specific components of RL algorithms, including action values and reward prediction errors (Frank and Claus, 2006; Niv, 2009; Lee et al., 2012; O'Doherty et al., 2015; Glimcher, 2011; Garrison et al., 2013; Dayan and Niv, 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Many current research practices are implicitly based on the interpretability and generalizability of computational model parameters.
source: Many current research practices are implicitly based on the interpretability and generalizability of computational model parameters (despite the fact that many researchers explicitly distance themselves from them).
evidence: This is an observation about research practices in the field.

claim: A model variable is generalizable if it is consistent across uses, such that a person would be characterized with the same values independent of the specific model or task used to estimate the variable.
source: For our purposes, we define a model variable (e.g. fitted parameter) as generalizable if it is consistent across uses, such that a person would be characterized with the same values independent of the specific model or task used to estimate the variable.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors for the purposes of this study.

claim: A model variable is interpretable if it isolates specific and unique cognitive elements, and/or is implemented in separable and unique neural substrates.
source: We define a model variable as interpretable if it isolates specific and unique cognitive elements, and/or is implemented in separable and unique neural substrates.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors for the purposes of this study.

claim: Some developmental studies have shown that learning rates increased with age.
source: For example, some developmental studies have shown that learning rates increased with age (Master et al., 2020; Davidow et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some developmental studies have shown that learning rates decrease with age.
source: whereas others have shown that they decrease (Decker et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Some developmental studies have reported U-shaped trajectories of learning rates with either peaks during adolescence.
source: Yet others have reported U-shaped trajectories with either peaks (Rosenbaum et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Some developmental studies have reported U-shaped trajectories of learning rates with troughs during adolescence.
source: or troughs (Eckstein et al., 2022) during adolescence
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Some developmental studies have reported stability of learning rates within the adolescent age range.
source: or stability within this age range (Palminteri et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The three learning tasks used in the study varied on several common dimensions, including feedback stochasticity, task volatility, and memory demands.
source: The three learning tasks we used varied on several common dimensions, including feedback stochasticity, task volatility, and memory demands (Figure 1E)
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is illustrated in Figure 1E.

claim: The tasks used in the study have been used previously to study RL processes.
source: and have been used previously to study RL processes (Davidow et al., 2016; Collins and Frank, 2012; Javadi et al., 2014; Master et al., 2020; Eckstein et al., 2022; Xia et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The tasks likely engaged other cognitive processes besides RL, such as working memory and reasoning.
source: However, like many tasks in the literature, the tasks likely also engaged other cognitive processes besides RL, such as working memory and reasoning.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of the tasks.

claim: Task A required participants to learn the correct associations between each of four stimuli (butterflies) and two responses (flowers) based on probabilistic feedback.
source: Task A required participants to learn the correct associations between each of four stimuli (butterflies) and two responses (flowers) based on probabilistic feedback (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the task design and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The best-fitting model for Task A contained three free parameters: learning rate from positive outcomes α+, inverse decision temperature β, and forgetting F.
source: The best-fitting model contained three free parameters: learning rate from positive outcomes α+, inverse decision temperature β, and forgetting F.
evidence: This describes the computational model used for Task A.

claim: Task B required participants to adapt to unexpected switches in the action-outcome contingencies of a simple bandit task based on semi-probabilistic feedback.
source: Task B required participants to adapt to unexpected switches in the action-outcome contingencies of a simple bandit task (only one of two boxes contained a gold coin at any time) based on semi-probabilistic feedback (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the task design and is illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Task C required learning of stimulus-response associations over several task blocks with varying numbers of stimuli, using deterministic feedback.
source: Task C required learning of stimulus-response associations like task A, but over several task blocks with varying numbers of stimuli, and using deterministic feedback (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes the task design and is illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Forgetting was significantly higher in task C than task A.
source: Forgetting was significantly higher in task C (mean: 0.19, sd: 0.17) than A (mean: 0.056, sd: 0.028).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with descriptive statistics provided.

claim: Task B was best fit without forgetting.
source: Task B was best fit without forgetting.
evidence: This is a finding from the model comparison and selection process.

claim: For all parameters, absolute parameter values differed substantially between tasks.
source: For all parameters, absolute parameter values hence differed substantially between tasks.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the data analysis.

claim: The three tasks produced significantly different estimates of learning rates, decision noise/exploration, and forgetting for the same participants.
source: This shows that the three tasks produced significantly different estimates of learning rates, decision noise/exploration, and forgetting for the same participants (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a summary finding from the data analysis, illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: Parameter differences echoed specific task demands: Learning rates and noise/exploration were highest in task B, where frequent switches required quick updating and high levels of exploration.
source: Interestingly, these parameter differences echoed specific task demands: Learning rates and noise/exploration were highest in task B, where frequent switches required quick updating and high levels of exploration.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to task characteristics.

claim: Forgetting was highest in task C, which posed the largest memory demands.
source: Similarly, forgetting was highest in task C, which posed the largest memory demands.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to task characteristics.

claim: Both α+ and noise/exploration parameters were significantly positively correlated between tasks A and B as well as between tasks A and C.
source: Indeed, both α+ (Appendix 8—figure 1A) and noise/exploration parameters (Appendix 8—figure 1B) were significantly positively correlated between tasks A and B as well as between tasks A and C.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis, with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Significant correlations of α+ and noise/exploration parameters were lacking between tasks B and C.
source: Significant correlations were lacking between tasks B and C.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: Both α+ and noise/exploration generalized in terms of the relationships they captured between participants, but only when tasks were sufficiently similar.
source: This suggests that both α+ and noise/exploration generalized in terms of the relationships they captured between participants; however, this generalization was only evident between tasks A and B or A and C, potentially due to the fact that task A was more similar to tasks B and C than these were to each other (Figure 1E; also see section 'Main axes of variation').
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation findings in relation to task similarity.

claim: Noise parameters generalized between tasks A and C despite differences in parameterization (ϵ vs. 1/β), showing robustness in the characterization of choice stochasticity.
source: Note that noise parameters generalized between tasks A and C despite differences in parameterization (ϵ vs. 1/β), showing robustness in the characterization of choice stochasticity (Appendix 8—figure 1B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation findings, with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: The fact that α− patterns are opposites of each other was reflected in the significant interaction terms of the overall regression model.
source: The fact that these patterns are opposites of each other was reflected in the significant interaction terms of the overall regression model (Table 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis, with reference to a table.

claim: For α+, adding task as a predictor did not improve model fit, suggesting that α+ showed similar age trajectories across tasks.
source: For α+, adding task as a predictor did not improve model fit, suggesting that α+ showed similar age trajectories across tasks (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis, with reference to a table.

claim: For noise/exploration and forgetting parameters, adding task as a predictor did not improve model fit, suggesting similar age trajectories across tasks.
source: For noise/exploration and forgetting parameters, adding task as a predictor also did not improve model fit (Table 2), suggesting similar age trajectories across tasks.
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis, with reference to a table.

claim: For decision noise/exploration, the grand model revealed a linear decrease and tapering off with age.
source: For decision noise/exploration, the grand model revealed a linear decrease and tapering off with age (Figure 2C; Table 3), in accordance with previous findings (Nussenbaum and Hartley, 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis, with reference to a figure and table, and citation to prior literature.

claim: For forgetting, the grand model did not reveal any age effects, suggesting inconsistent or lacking developmental changes.
source: For forgetting, the grand model did not reveal any age effects (Figure 2C; Table 3), suggesting inconsistent or lacking developmental changes.
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis, with reference to a figure and table.

claim: For both α+ and noise/exploration parameters, task A predicted tasks B and C, and tasks B and C predicted task A, but tasks B and C did not predict each other.
source: For both α+ and noise/exploration parameters, task A predicted tasks B and C, and tasks B and C predicted task A, but tasks B and C did not predict each other (Table 4; Figure 2D)
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis, with reference to a table and figure.

claim: For forgetting, tasks A and C were not predictive of each other.
source: For forgetting, tasks A and C were not predictive of each other (Table 4)
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis, with reference to a table.

claim: All parameters differed significantly between tasks in terms of absolute values.
source: To summarize, (1) all parameters differed significantly between tasks in terms of absolute values (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the data analysis.

claim: Absolute parameter values varied more between tasks than between participants within tasks, suggesting that task demands played a larger role in determining parameter values than participants' individual characteristics.
source: Intriguingly, absolute parameter values varied more between tasks than between participants within tasks, suggesting that task demands played a larger role in determining parameter values than participants' individual characteristics.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Task identity did not affect the age trajectories of noise/exploration, forgetting, or learning rate α+.
source: Task identity did not affect the age trajectories of noise/exploration, forgetting, or learning rate α+ (Figure 2C), suggesting possible generalization.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the data analysis.

claim: Only noise/exploration and α+ age trajectories were the same between tasks, and this was only possible when tasks were sufficiently similar.
source: However, only noise/exploration and α+ age trajectories were the same between tasks, hence revealing deeper similarities, and this was only possible when tasks were sufficiently similar (Table 4), highlighting the limits of generalization.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the data analysis.

claim: Generalizability of all other task combinations and parameters was significantly lower than expected from a perfectly-generalizing population.
source: Generalizability of all other task combinations and parameters was significantly lower than expected from a perfectly-generalizing population.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the comparison with simulated agents.

claim: For the parameters whose age trajectories showed signs of generalization, the results replicated patterns in the literature, with noise/exploration decreasing and α+ increasing from childhood to early adulthood.
source: (4) For the parameters whose age trajectories showed signs of generalization, our results replicated patterns in the literature, with noise/exploration decreasing and α+ increasing from childhood to early adulthood (Nussenbaum and Hartley, 2019).
evidence: This is a summary of findings with citation to prior literature.

claim: PC1 captured a range of 'good', task-engaged behaviors, and is likely similar to the construct of 'decision acuity'.
source: PC1 therefore captured a range of 'good', task-engaged behaviors, and is likely similar to the construct of 'decision acuity' (Moutoussis et al., 2021)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PCA results with citation to prior literature.

claim: PC1 increased significantly with age, consistent with increasing performance.
source: Like decision acuity Moutoussis et al., 2021, our PC1 increased significantly with age, consistent with increasing performance (Appendix 3—figure 1B; age effects of subsequent PCs in Appendix 8—figure 4; Appendix 8—table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis, with reference to supplementary figures and tables.

claim: In all three tasks, noise/exploration and forgetting parameters loaded negatively on PC1, showing that elevated decision stochasticity and the decay of learned information were associated with poorer performance in all tasks.
source: In all three tasks, noise/exploration and forgetting parameters loaded negatively on PC1 (Figure 3A), showing that elevated decision stochasticity and the decay of learned information were associated with poorer performance in all tasks.
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: α+ showed positive loadings on PC1 throughout, suggesting that faster integration of positive feedback was associated with better performance in all tasks.
source: α+ showed positive loadings throughout, suggesting that faster integration of positive feedback was associated with better performance in all tasks.
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis.

claim: Noise/exploration, forgetting, and α+ showed consistency across tasks in terms of their interpretation with respect to decision acuity.
source: Taken together, noise/exploration, forgetting, and α+ showed consistency across tasks in terms of their interpretation with respect to decision acuity.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the PCA findings.

claim: PC2 and PC3 encoded task contrasts: PC2 contrasted task B to task C, and PC3 contrasted task A to both B and C.
source: This revealed that PC2 and PC3 encoded task contrasts: PC2 contrasted task B to task C (loadings were positive / negative / near-zero for corresponding features of tasks B / C / A; Figure 3B). PC3 contrasted task A to both B and C (loadings were positive / negative for corresponding features on task A / tasks B and C; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: The ordering of PC2 before PC3 shows that participants' behavior differed more between task B compared to C than between B and C compared to A.
source: The ordering of PC2 before PC3 shows that participants' behavior differed more between task B compared to C (PC2: 8.9% explained variance) than between B and C compared to A (PC3: 6.2%; Appendix 8—figure 4), as expected based on task similarity (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PCA results in relation to task similarity.

claim: These parameters were clearly distinguishable between tasks, showing that they did not capture the same processes.
source: In other words, these parameters were clearly distinguishable between tasks, showing that they did not capture the same processes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PCA findings.

claim: Each parameter captured sufficient task-specific variance to indicate in which task it was measured.
source: What is more, each parameter captured sufficient task-specific variance to indicate in which task it was measured.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PCA findings.

claim: The emerging major axes of variation in the large dataset were task engagement (PC1) and task differences (PC2-PC3), together capturing 40.2% of explained variance.
source: Taken together, the PCA revealed that the emerging major axes of variation in our large dataset, together capturing 40.2% of explained variance, were task engagement (PC1) and task differences (PC2-PC3).
evidence: This is a summary of the PCA findings.

claim: Task engagement / decision acuity (PC1) played a crucial role for all four parameters, and this role was consistent across tasks for noise/exploration, forgetting, and α+.
source: Task engagement / decision acuity (PC1) played a crucial role for all four parameters (Figure 3A), and this role was consistent across tasks for noise/exploration, forgetting, and α+.
evidence: This is a summary of the PCA findings.

claim: All significant coefficients in the Ridge regression connected tasks A and B or tasks A and C but never tasks B and C, mirroring previous results with regard to task similarity.
source: Assessing general patterns that arose in this analysis, we found that all significant coefficients connected tasks A and B or tasks A and C but never tasks B and C, mirroring previous results (Figure 2D; section 'Relative parameter differences') with regard to task similarity (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from the Ridge regression analysis.

claim: No parameter had a specific core that extended across all three tasks—the largest shared variance encompassed two tasks.
source: This suggests that no parameter had a specific core that extended across all three tasks—the largest shared variance encompassed two tasks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Ridge regression findings.

claim: Coefficients were significant when predicting noise/exploration in task A from noise/exploration in tasks B or C, but the inverse was not true.
source: Focusing on noise/exploration parameters, coefficients were significant when predicting noise/exploration in task A from noise/exploration in tasks B or C, but the inverse was not true, such that coefficients were not significant when predicting tasks B or C from task A (Figure 4A; Table 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the Ridge regression analysis.

claim: Noise/exploration parameters captured variance in task A that they also captured in tasks B and C, but also captured additional cognitive processes in tasks B and C that they did not capture in task A.
source: The first result implies parameter specificity, showing that noise/exploration parameters captured variance (cognitive processes) in task A that they also captured in tasks B and C. The second result, however, implies a lack of specificity, showing that noise/exploration parameters captured additional cognitive processes in tasks B and C that they did not capture in task A.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Ridge regression findings.

claim: The variance that both B and C captured in A was not the same: Prediction accuracy increased when combining tasks B and C to predict task A.
source: A further lack of specificity was evident in that even the variance that both B and C captured in A was not the same: Prediction accuracy increased when combining tasks B and C to predict task A, showing that noise/exploration parameters in tasks B and C captured partly non-overlapping aspects of noise/exploration (Figure 4B, left-most set of bars, compare purple to orange and blue).
evidence: This is a finding from the Ridge regression analysis.

claim: When predicting α+ in task B, no parameter of any task showed a significant coefficient, and it was impossible to predict variance in task B's α+ even when combining all parameters of the other tasks.
source: However, a lack of specificity was evident in task B: When predicting α+ in task B, no parameter of any task showed a significant coefficient (including α+ in other tasks; Table 5), and it was impossible to predict variance in task B's α+ even when combining all parameters of the other tasks (Figure 4B, 'Task B' panel).
evidence: This is a finding from the Ridge regression analysis.

claim: α+ captured fundamentally different cognitive processes in task B compared to the other tasks.
source: This reveals that α+ captured fundamentally different cognitive processes in task B compared to the other tasks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Ridge regression findings.

claim: Learning rates in task B did not capture the same core of cognitive processes compared to other tasks.
source: This reveals a fundamental lack of specificity, implying that learning rates in task B did not capture the same core of cognitive processes compared to other tasks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Ridge regression findings.

claim: Processes that were captured by noise/exploration parameters in task A were captured by different parameters in other tasks, such that noise/exploration parameters did not capture distinct cognitive processes.
source: This shows that processes that were captured by noise/exploration parameters in task A were captured by different parameters in other tasks, such that noise/exploration parameters did not capture distinct cognitive processes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Ridge regression findings.

claim: α+ in task A was predicted nonspecifically by all parameters of task B (with the notable exception of α+ itself).
source: In the case of learning rates, α+ in task A was predicted nonspecifically by all parameters of task B (with the notable exception of α+ itself; Figure 4A; Table 5)
evidence: This is a finding from the Ridge regression analysis.

claim: The cognitive processes that α+ captured in task A were captured by an interplay of several parameters in task B.
source: suggesting that the cognitive processes that α+ captured in task A were captured by an interplay of several parameters in task B.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Ridge regression findings.

claim: Task A's α+ was predicted by task C's working memory parameters ρ and K.
source: Furthermore, task A's α+ was predicted by task C's working memory parameters ρ and K (Figure 4A; Table 5)
evidence: This is a finding from the Ridge regression analysis.

claim: α+ captured a conglomerate of RL and working memory processes in task A that was isolated by different parameters in task C.
source: suggesting that α+ captured a conglomerate of RL and working memory processes in task A that was isolated by different parameters in task C (Collins and Frank, 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Ridge regression findings with citation to prior literature.

claim: No variance in task C's working memory parameters could be explained by any other parameters.
source: In support of this interpretation, no variance in task C's working memory parameters could be explained by any other parameters (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is a finding from the Ridge regression analysis.

claim: Task C's working memory parameters captured unique working memory processes that were not captured by other parameters.
source: suggesting that they captured unique working memory processes that were not captured by other parameters.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Ridge regression findings.

claim: Task C's RL parameters could be explained by parameters in other tasks, suggesting they captured overlapping RL processes.
source: Task C's RL parameters, on the other hand, could be explained by parameters in other tasks (Figure 4B), suggesting they captured overlapping RL processes.
evidence: This is a finding from the Ridge regression analysis with interpretation.

claim: In the case of noise/exploration, there was evidence for both specificity and a lack thereof (mutual prediction between some, but not all noise/exploration parameters).
source: In sum, in the case of noise/exploration, there was evidence for both specificity and a lack thereof (mutual prediction between some, but not all noise/exploration parameters).
evidence: This is a summary of the Ridge regression findings.

claim: Noise/exploration parameters were also not perfectly distinct, being predicted by a small set of other parameters from different tasks.
source: Noise/exploration parameters were also not perfectly distinct, being predicted by a small set of other parameters from different tasks.
evidence: This is a summary of the Ridge regression findings.

claim: In the case of learning rates, some specificity was evident in the shared variance between tasks A and C, but that specificity was missing in task B.
source: In the case of learning rates, some specificity was evident in the shared variance between tasks A and C, but that specificity was missing in task B.
evidence: This is a summary of the Ridge regression findings.

claim: Distinctiveness was particularly low for learning rates, with variance shared widely between multiple different parameters.
source: Distinctiveness was particularly low for learning rates, with variance shared widely between multiple different parameters.
evidence: This is a summary of the Ridge regression findings.

claim: Because different tasks elicited different behaviors, and because each behavior was captured by the same parameter across tasks, parameters necessarily differed between tasks.
source: This suggests a succinct explanation for why parameters did not generalize between tasks: Because different tasks elicited different behaviors (Appendix 3—figure 1B), and because each behavior was captured by the same parameter across tasks (Figure 4C), parameters necessarily differed between tasks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Exploration/noise parameters showed considerable generalizability in the form of correlated variance and age trajectories.
source: Exploration/noise parameters showed considerable generalizability in the form of correlated variance and age trajectories.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The decline in exploration/noise between ages 8–17 was consistent with previous studies.
source: Furthermore, the decline in exploration/noise we observed between ages 8–17 was consistent with previous studies (Nussenbaum and Hartley, 2019; Somerville et al., 2017; Gopnik, 2020)
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings with citations to prior literature.

claim: For 2/3 pairs of tasks, the degree of generalization of exploration/noise parameters was significantly below the level of generalization expected by agents with perfect generalization.
source: Still, for 2/3 pairs of tasks, the degree of generalization was significantly below the level of generalization expected by agents with perfect generalization.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: While exploration/noise parameters were generalizable across tasks, they were not neurocognitively interpretable.
source: Thus, while exploration/noise parameters were generalizable across tasks, they were not neurocognitively "interpretable" (as defined above).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Learning rate from negative feedback showed a substantial lack of generalizability: parameters were less consistent within participants than within tasks, and age trajectories differed both quantitatively and qualitatively.
source: Learning rate from negative feedback showed a substantial lack of generalizability: parameters were less consistent within participants than within tasks, and age trajectories differed both quantitatively and qualitatively.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Learning rates from positive feedback showed some convincing patterns of generalization.
source: Learning rates from positive feedback, however, showed some convincing patterns of generalization.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The study confirms the patterns of generalizable exploration/noise parameters and task-specific learning rate parameters that are emerging from the literature.
source: Taken together, our study confirms the patterns of generalizable exploration/noise parameters and task-specific learning rate parameters that are emerging from the literature (Nussenbaum and Hartley, 2019).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings with citation to prior literature.

claim: The same participants will show different parameters when tested using different tasks.
source: Furthermore, we show that this is not a result of between-participant comparisons, but that the same participants will show different parameters when tested using different tasks.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The inconsistency of learning rate parameters leads to the conclusion that we cannot measure an individual's 'intrinsic learning rate'.
source: The inconsistency of learning rate parameters leads to the important conclusion that we cannot measure an individual's 'intrinsic learning rate', and that we should not draw general conclusions about 'the development of learning rates' with the implication that they apply to all contexts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: Discrepancies in the literature are expected even with a consistent methodological pipeline and up-to-date modeling techniques, because they are an expected consequence of variations in context.
source: Our results show that discrepancies are expected even with a consistent methodological pipeline and up-to-date modeling techniques, because they are an expected consequence of variations in context (e.g. features of the experimental task [section Parameters and behavior] and the computational model).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: Analysis of model parameters alone does not permit unequivocal conclusions about cognitive processes if the context varies.
source: Under this view, analysis of model parameters alone does not permit unequivocal conclusions about cognitive processes if the context varies (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: The interpretation of model parameter results requires careful contextualization.
source: and the interpretation of model parameter results requires careful contextualization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: Future research needs to investigate context factors to characterize these issues in more detail.
source: Future research needs to investigate context factors to characterize these issues in more detail.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: The systematic investigation of task space could elucidate the relationships between parameter generalizability and task-based context factors.
source: For example, which task characteristics determine which parameters will generalize and which will not, and to what extent? Does context impact whether parameters capture overlapping versus distinct variance? Here, the systematic investigation of task space (i.e., testing the same participants on a large battery of learning tasks created as the full factorial of all task features) could elucidate the relationships between parameter generalizability and task-based context factors (e.g., stochasticity, volatility, reward probability).
